utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, I take it that it has been agreed upon not to sit on Monday next week, but instead to sit on Monday next -- the 28th of November. But I'm not sure it has been decided whether to sit in the morning or in the afternoon on the 28th. I have to ask Mr. Harvey whether it is okay with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. I'm grateful because this is an important religious holiday, a family holiday as well. As regards the Monday you mentioned, I will simply abide by your decision concerning whether we'll be sitting in the morning or in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, I'm on that one. Yes, Mr. President, we're sitting at 2.00 p.m. in the Haradinaj case on the 28th. It will certainly be convenient for me personally to sit in the morning, but if it's more convenient to the other parties, I can certainly arrange for my team to be fully represented if you would prefer to sit in the afternoon in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In consultation -- after having consultation with the other Chambers, we'll come back to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- as soon as possible. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue. Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday we finished off looking at the decision signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Sajic, 4th of May, ordering the general public mobilisation and setting a dead-line for weapons disarmament on 11 May. I want to continue on this topic, Mr. Brown, disarmament operations, disarmament dead-lines, and the military events which followed. This is primarily in pages 64 through 68 of your report, paragraphs 2.10 to 2.21, where you go into these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 17918 up, and while it's coming up, I'll say this is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina or Official Gazette of the ARK as we sometimes refer to it. And I would like to start off with page 1 just so we can see the document we're looking at. I want it in both English and the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do, Mr. Brown, is try to go through actually three different dates and decisions on weapons deadlines and then I'll ask you some questions about them, but stop me if you need to. Okay?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So here we are on page 1, we see that this is the Official Gazette and, in fact, that the Sajic decision is contained on the first page. It's replicated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could skip ahead two pages now to page 3 in the English which is page 2 in the B/C/S or Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There we see the decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff of the ARK dated 5th of May. Simply, the person listed at number 2, Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sajic, vice-president, is that the same Sajic who signed the decision we saw?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just as you said, we see that number 8, General Talic, is a member of this staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to page 5 in the English, page 3 of the Serbian. And we should have here the conclusions of the Crisis Staff from the 8th of May. And if we look at point 3: "Presidents of the National Defence councils are to report to the War Staff of the ARK about actions they ... have taken in order to disarm paramilitary units ..." et cetera. And that: "The strictest of sanctions will be imposed on those who refuse to return weapons." And we also see that at one-hour intervals, Banja Luka radio is to broadcast announcements to citizens to return weapons so that peace can be maintained. I'm slightly paraphrasing there. Moving on now to page 15 -- sorry, page 15, yes, of the English, page 7 of the Serbian. This is a decision you talk about in your report, the extension of the weapons dead-line. We see at the 11th of May, the original date of the dead-line, the ARK Crisis Staff extended the dead-line to the 14th of May, 1992, and explains their reasoning, which I won't read out, in the second paragraph. And then the third paragraph again states that when the dead-line expires, weapons will be confiscated by employees of the security services centre of the ARK and severe sanctions will be imposed on those who ignore the call of the Crisis Staff. And let me stop there and ask you: Do you recall discussing in your report the way the military was apprised of or concerned with these weapons deadlines, if you could explain that briefly?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of -- at least one that I remember offhand but references in the 1st Krajina Corps documents, indicating that they -- in a daily combat report that they made reference to these dead-lines. So presumably because General Talic or a member of his staff were attending the Crisis Staff meetings, they most likely became aware of those dead-lines and made reference to them in their own reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll get to that one in a minute. If I could now go to page 21 of the English, page 9 of the Serbian. This is conclusions from the 18th of May meeting. We're now past the extended dead-line of the 14th of May. And here we see the conclusion number 3 that: "Illegally obtained weapons will be taken away by members of the military and civilian police." And: "All those that are not part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina or its police must return their weapons," et cetera. Did in fact -- and you speak about this in your report. Did the weapons dead-lines and the confiscation of weapons, we see here now the Crisis Staff has mentioned the military's involvement, did those dead-lines and these conclusions play a role in military -- subsequent military operations in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I think initially the first few references seemed to indicate that there was only going to be the police that were going to be involved in the operations, but then after that from -- from this time on, it makes reference to the police and the military will be taking part in these operations. And, in fact, the military did take part. From the documents I've seen of the Krajina Corps, they took part in a number of operations to -- which they termed to disarm paramilitaries in Prijedor, in Sanski Most, in Kotor Varos later on and Kljuc, certainly in the 1st Krajina Corps area, and others actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was disarmament ever discussed as a reason or justification for a military operation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some cases they justified that as the reason. There are a number of reasons they give through the summer, but this is certainly one of them. Mopping-up or cleansing the territory is another, taking control of territory is another. But certainly around this time in some of the municipalities, they couched the operations they were taking part in as operations to disarm paramilitaries or those in the possession of illegally held weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these pages. I will come back to another conclusion from the ARK Crisis Staff later, so I -- I'm not sure whether it's best to give this one number or to separate it. It's -- whichever is the most convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that this is just of 23 pages, why don't we admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it has been translated in full?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3924, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could now have, please, 65 ter 00478.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I may have jumped the gun a bit by asking some questions, Mr. Brown. This relates to what we've just been talking about. It's the 12th of May, therefore it's still stamped as 5th Corps command, the same day as the 16th Assembly Session, to the military district, signed by General Talic. And can you just discuss -- this is included in your report at page -- at footnote 267. And can you explain why this is significant.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 3, at the end of that paragraph, it makes note that the dead-line has been extended. Maybe this is what I was talking about, that the Krajina -- sorry, the 5th Corps, 1st Krajina Corps were aware of the decisions that were being implemented in the ARK area and they're -- they obviously think it's of importance because they're sending it up their own chain to their next headquarters. There is another reference on the second page. It's not necessarily to do specifically with the ARK dead-lines -- well, it is in part, but it notes that the political and security situation is deteriorating in the area of Bosanski Novi. The day before the 12th, there had been operations in Bosanski Novi which, again, are linked to the chain of documents about mobilisation and disarming that came from Bogdan Subotic's decision on the 16th of April and the ARK decisions earlier in May. So Bosanski Novi was one of the municipalities that I saw where disarmament was quite early, and in fact Bosanski Novi was referenced in passing by one of the delegates in the 16th Assembly Session, which of course takes place on the 12th of May -- in fact, the delegate from Krupa who talked about the fact that Muslims had left Krupa had visited Novi the day before, on the 11th, and in the Assembly session makes reference to the fact that there is operations going on there. So disarmament was going on from around this time, even though in some of the other municipalities, for example, in Prijedor, it was a bit later in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, were you referring to Miroslav Vjestica?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the speaker in the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3925, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You spoke about Prijedor. I'd like to go there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit D01542, please. These are some documents between the Banja Luka security services centre and the Prijedor public security centre which are bundled together. Your Honours will see that the dates go backwards to an extent from the top pages, from the 25th of May back towards the 14th of May. And so perhaps it would be simplest to first just page through these documents in e-court and see what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then I'll ask you a question, Mr. Brown. And again, this is an exhibit so I'll be quite quick. The first is the 25th of May reply from the Prijedor chief, Drljaca. And what does it say here - you reference this in your report - about the involvement of the military in disarmament?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this in terms of the time was after -- Hambarine, I think, had been attacked first, but it's around that time in the middle of the operations in Prijedor. And as I said earlier, the original disarmament plan was to involve predominantly the CSB but later on it was amended that the military were involved. And here it seems to be indicating at the time of the operation -- that the operations are ongoing, that the military are working with the police in implementing the plan or at least in part and that they'd seized a number of weapons during these operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I note that two documents seem to be different. The B/C/S version is written by Zupljanin and the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then I think we've got the -- it must be the second page of the B/C/S because there is -- you're correct, Your Honour, I'm sorry. There is one document that looks very similar -- there is the correct one. Thank you. This is the reply to Chief Zupljanin. If we could go to the next page in each, please -- perhaps the prior page, then, in the Serbian. Yes. And the next page in the English, please, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There we see the Zupljanin correspondence of the same day to all public security stations, referencing his earlier order, asking for information. If we continue now to the next page, the Banja Luka security services document from 14 May. And that is correct, there is a stamp for the 25th of May on the top but the document is dated 14 May. So now this document is the date of the extended dead-line. It reads: "In keeping with the decision of the autonomous region of Bosnian Krajina regarding the surrender of illegally owned weapons ..." citing to the Crisis Staff conclusions orders the making of concrete plans for the seizure of illegally owned weapons. And can you just tell us why you included this document in your report. It's the same theme about military activities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be a natural follow-on from the ARK decision, to make concrete plans, and the -- Mr. Zupljanin, as the senior policeman in the area, is disseminating that instruction down to his subordinates to say: You are to do that. And it also makes reference that activity can be implemented by authorised officials and the military police of the Banja Luka corps. So this seems to indicate that there was more of an engagement of the military from this period onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And very quickly, if we can go to another document that's already an exhibit, P03529. Same time-period, minutes of the Council for National Defence of Prijedor Municipal Assembly, 15 May at 10.00 a.m. You cited this report -- this -- these minutes in your report at footnotes 281 and 324. And if we go to page 2, please, where we speak about mobilisation in the municipality at item 2 and 3 at the top and, below number 4, disarmament of paramilitary formations. Can you first just tell us who the military personnel are that are present during these minutes and, again, why -- why this document's significant.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting is attended by Colonel Vladimir Arsic, Your Honours, who was the commander of the 343rd Brigade, sometimes called the 43rd Brigade -- or later called the 43rd Brigade. He was also commander of what was called Ops Group Prijedor which was, if you like, the military command headquarters for all the military units in the Prijedor area, wider Prijedor area. So he's concurrently the brigade commander and concurrently the Operations Prijedor commander, so the senior military figure in the area. Pero Colic, Colonel Pero Colic was a brigade commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade which was another big brigade based in Prijedor. Both brigades had fought in Western Slavonia and both had returned in April and a bit later as well, April/May time, from Western Slavonia. And Pero Colic was the brigade commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade, the second main brigade in Prijedor. Slobodan Kuruzovic was the TO commander in Prijedor. I think he remained in that position until early June when the TOs were integrated into the VRS as has been expected to happen from the announcements in 16th Assembly Session. So he was the TO commander. Radmilo Zeljaja was the 43rd deputy commander, so he is Colonel Arsic's deputy. And then obviously the remaining members of the meeting are the senior civilian SDS municipal figures and Mr. Simo Drljaca who was the chief of police. So it's a military/police/civilian meeting, Crisis Staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we just see at the bottom of the page there, under item 4 -- sorry, item 4.1 below, if we could go to the very bottom of the page, the army command in Prijedor is actually tasked at this meeting with participating in drafting the plan of disarmament?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so presumably the police and the military are involved in implementing the plan that was discussed and issued from the ARK decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to move on --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just -- and obviously the plan was put into operation, at least in part, as you can see from the prior document from the CSB of the 25th, where they say: We implement it in part but because of ongoing operations, it wasn't completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to -- still moving on chronologically, as you've just discussed, the putting in place of these plans and the events that followed during this disarmament period and the combat operations in May, June, and some of the common features you talk about, if I could go to D01743, a 1KK document from 27 May 1992. You cite this several places in your report, this report on the elimination of Green Berets in the wider area of Kozarac. I'll just ask very simply: What do you see? Why have you included this in your report and why did you believe it was an important document to talk about?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's a good document, highlighting that the operation -- there was a military operation in Kozarac, that it involved the -- a number of key units from the 1st Krajina Corps. It talks about the engagement of the 343rd Brigade or at least a part of it, that is Colonel Arsic's unit, and a large battalion was involved. It talks about the support of two 105-millimetre howitzer batteries. Those batteries had been moved in to Prijedor in the early days of May on an instruction from the corps. And also that there was the engagement of an M-84 tank squadron. The M-84 tank was the most advanced tank that the Yugoslav Army had at that time and a squadron is usually up to about 12 tanks. It makes reference to what they call the Green Beret's strength between 1.500 and 2.000 men, although my reading of this is that this was not the figure of armed men that they were -- that they were up against. There's other documents that would seem to indicate that what armed elements there was less than this. But they say that there's -- without any heavy weapons. And then it talks about the areas that they -- that they -- the operation took place in and that there has been quite a large number of people captured. But it also mentions that the 1KK did themselves take some casualties and that did happen. There was an incident at the early stage of the operation in which soldiers were killed. So it's clear that this incident was of importance for General Talic, for him to report on it up to his chain of command. And the date is also of some importance in that it's the 27th of May, so the operation didn't last long. I think it started on the 25th, as it says here, and it was finished by the 27th. So it wasn't a long -- particularly long operation for them. There had been a prior operation at Hambarine, I believe on the 22nd to 24th or 22nd to 23rd, again in which a couple of soldiers were killed. But it's clear that for General Talic to write this instruction it's of some importance to him to send up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, continuing in this period, P03656, please, another 1KK command report from the 1st of June now, a few days later, 1992. This one again signed by the person we talked about yesterday, Colonel Vukelic. And this goes back now - while it's coming up - to the army's -- the VRS's knowledge and connection to the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff. Can you please tell us about this document. And I'll note -- sorry, I should say that on your report at page 49, paragraph 1.13 for everybody, you talk there about the 1KK's connection to the ARK Crisis Staff and that Talic had members of the 1KK attend ARK Crisis Staff meetings. Sorry to interrupt you there, but if you could just tell us about this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is another -- well, it is another document that summarises the activities of the corps in the preceding period and it comes, if you like, two or three weeks after the Assembly session. I believe Mr. Vukelic -- Colonel Vukelic had written another report in between -- I think it went out on the 26th as well. But this one comes, in essence, after a number of the attacks in the municipalities had occurred, those being in Prijedor, operations in Sanski Most at this time, and Kljuc also. And the report summarises from their perspective what has happened in those areas. So, for example, halfway down the first page, it summarises in that paragraph the operations in Kljuc. It makes mention that there was an attack on a JNA or a military column that was returning from Knin which occurred and killed a number of soldiers. It makes reference to about eight or ten Green Berets in the area, but that the energetic action by the 30th Partisan Division resulted in the defeat and break-up of those forces in the town of Kljuc itself and the villages of Pudin Han, Velagic, and Donji Ramici, and that the corps units had established full control of the area. It makes mention that weapons had been seized and some 280 soldiers captured in Kljuc. Operations in Kljuc were still ongoing in this time. I think they continued for another day or two. The next paragraph discusses the operations in or at least summarises operations in Sanski Most. It talks about heavy fire from the area of Kamicak and Vrhpolje against positions of the 6th Brigade. That was the brigade, Colonel Basara's brigade that I mentioned yesterday, but that in that area the brigade took control, captured 30 Muslim extremists without any casualties. The next paragraphs summarise what had happened in Prijedor in the preceding days. It makes mention that there had been fighting there, heavy fighting in Hambarine, Prijedor, and Kozarac, but that troops in the area had, again, been involved. It makes mention that the troops had arrested more than 2.000 Green Berets who were now in Omarska, 135 were in Stara Gradiska prison, that was a military prison that had been used in the war in Croatia, and that 5.000 were in Trnopolje. So they seemed to portray anybody who was put into these detention centres as Green Berets. It makes mention, again, of the 43rd Brigade, a seasoned unit and that they were excelling, and that commendations or a commendation from the corps commander was going to be disseminated to them. So of note, he says: "The 43rd Brigade are an example of how one should act when defending the SRBH." And it does make mention, as I said before, that the -- there were some casualties in the operations in Prijedor from the VRS side. So it's clear that a large number of people have been rounded up or captured in that operation and that the corps is aware that they have been sent to Omarska, Stara Gradiska, and Trnopolje. A little bit later down in the report, it makes mention of some of the other areas in the corps, but the second-to-last paragraph on the same page makes reference to Kotor Varos, which at that time hadn't seen military action. It saw it a little bit later, but it notes in Kotor Varos that the -- some of the forces from the 122nd Brigade, which was the VRS unit in that area, had sealed off Kotor Varos. There were some armed extremists want -- "armed operations while some decent Muslims were in favour of peaceful coexistence with the Serbs. A hundred families from this town have requested to move out to Nova Gradiska. No armed provocations have occurred so far, although the estimate is that there are about 5- to 7.000 armed Muslims and Ustashas in the municipality." It seems a rather large number and whether it's just their, again, potentially couching anybody who is against the VRS as an extremist. On page 3 of the English, at the very top, it notes: "The municipalities of Bosanska Gradiska, Srbac, Laktasi, and Prnjavor are stable, and Muslim and Croatian extremists have started handing in their weapons." So it would seem that the weapons deadline issue and the plans were not just for Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc but were wider than that and included other municipalities in the ARK area. There is another reference not necessarily directed to the operations themselves, but it notes, if we go back to paragraph 1 -- sorry, page 1, in relation to Banja Luka and also the wider ARK area, it notes: "In the Banja Luka region, such forces have been completed isolated for the time being," that's enemy forces, "and individuals and groups are being disarmed every day, particularly within the city itself," again presumably part of this operation to disarm. "Persons who fail to respond to mobilisation or work duty lose their jobs and criminal prosecution is instigated against them." I believe that was probably related to one of the ARK decisions slightly earlier than this. It notes: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the Region of Bosnian Krajina has issued decisions to facilitate such departures, providing that Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." I believe this is also linked to an ARK decision which had happened a few days before this, but it would seem to me to be clear that the 1KK knows that Muslims and Croats are moving out, but that they shouldn't be allowed to do so unless Serbs can move in and they at least interpreted those decisions as -- that those who are leaving are not going to be able to come back. It's also of note that this document is another one at the end that is annotated it's to be disseminated and passed down to units of the corps in order for them to be informed of the situation. And I think this may be of some importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could go back to what we had as 65 ter 17918. We'd put in the 23 pages, but I need to go a little bit further to page 41 of the English. This is again the ARK Crisis Staff gazette, and page 18 to 19 -- bottom of page 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move to that document. The previous document which is before us is the one which has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the page numbers seem to be different. There are additional pages at the end in B/C/S. Could you take a look into it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You referred to this decision, I think, the one that will be coming up, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be the conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff for 29 May 1992, again page 41 of the English, bottom of page 18 in the Serbian language. Again, that was 65 ter 17918. That's correct on the English. Bottom of page 18 in the Serbian version. Okay. Now we need to go back to page 41 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, if you can just take a look at this conclusion from 29 May 1992, just a few days before the June 1st 1KK document we looked at. Is this a document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document that -- that it would appear to be that the meeting was held on the 29th and the military were clearly aware of it. This is the document that -- or this is the conclusion, I think, that is referenced in Vukelic's instruction that -- his report on the 1st of June that -- and it, for me, cuts to this issue of resettlement. It has echos of what a number of the delegates said at the 16th Assembly Session, that the establishment of territory would involve the resettlement of people. And here there is a qualification that people are -- will only be allowed to leave as Serbs come in, into the Krajina. And from the 1st of June document, it's the military's interpretation that these people are not going to be able to come back. So I think it's linked to this issue that it's -- the Serb territory is going to be predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that, Your Honour, which was a bit further down in the same gazette that we've already put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only those pages, yes. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that it has been -- part of it has been admitted. Is it the same Official Gazette that we admitted in its entirety? I think it's different. Page numbers are different -- oh, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the same gazette, Your Honour, that we admitted earlier today, but only up to page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The actual gazette is a total of 51 pages in English. It's 23 pages in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For ease of reference, we'll admit it separately. Could you split it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- load it separately. We'll give it a separate number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P3926.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if I can make one more comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It strikes me that the ARK decision as well makes -- itself makes note that several thousand people from Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Novi had already, at least according to the decision, wished to move out. And bearing in mind that this is on the 29th of May, it seems a very short space of time for, all of a sudden, so many thousand people to wish to voluntarily leave their homes. And I think that -- the military document had already said on the 29th that there were 7.000 people in Trnopolje and Omarska. And it seems to me that this is -- you know, several thousand people in a very short space of time voluntarily wishing to leave seems unusual to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now moving on to the next day, 2nd of June, from the -- another 1KK document -- command document. This is not an exhibit. 65 ter 00545, please. You've cited this document several times in your report. Can you just tell us about how you see this document in relation to the 1KK operations, and in particular disarmament.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another daily combat report going to the Main Staff, and maybe I draw Your Honours' attention to a number of sections. In paragraph 1 there's a reference at the end, saying: "In Lisnja village, an armed conflict occurred between Muslim extremists and the army of the SR BiH. Some Muslim extremists were captured while a rather large number of them pulled out towards Crni Vrh." Lisnja is in Prnjavor municipality, I believe. There is another reference later in a combat report that the population of Lisnja are expelled. In the second paragraph it talks about the operations that are ongoing in the corps. It notes: "In Kljuc, around 900 persons have been captured in the course of the fighting around Kljuc and around 400 rifles seized in the process." The reference at the end of that paragraph says: "... because Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja has been expelled." And also in paragraph 3 it notes: "The wider area of Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Kljuc are under the control of our units." Again, the operations that they conducted they conducted quite quickly and at least in their reports are saying that the area is generally under control, although there were still sporadic incidents that followed this period. But in those municipalities, they themselves seemed to have the area under control quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit P3927.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether the translation is right, I don't know whether "expelled" would be the right word to be used for "iseljavanje." Generally speaking the translations leave much to be desired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Yes, with regard to the translation we'll -- we have another way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 04933, please, that's 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a MUP document from Sanski Most coming up from the 15th of June, so now a couple of weeks later. We'd spoken about, in the previous document, references to Sanski Most, Kljuc, that area. And this document is signed by the Sanski Most SJB chief, Mirko Vrucinic. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Nicholls. All the documents you are dealing with today must have been cited in one of his footnotes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify them for our reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this one is footnotes 340 and 452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And afterwards, if Your Honours -- if it would be helpful, where I haven't cited them, I -- and I'm sure my friend won't object, I could submit a list of footnote references for all the ones that we've talked about today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there would be no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, again, now this is a police document talking about the disarmament operations which have been underway, again looking back at May. Could you just discuss this with us briefly.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assuming what's happened here is that the Sanski Most police have been asked to provide a summary of what had happened in May, and it discusses the operations that happened in Sanski Most, the wider Sanski Most area, noting that the disarming and surrendering of weapons, it was carried out between the 10th and 25th of May, again presumably linked to the various decisions of the ARK and the CSBs to implement a disarming operation. But it notes that the -- this is in paragraph 1: "The Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons, but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered and were concealed (buried) on instructions from above." Then there clearly was an operation on the 25th, which they say: "There was a military action (attack) on the down-town neighbourhood of Mahala which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians, but no significant amounts of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier." They then make note of another operation in the Muslim villages of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, and on that occasion, a Muslim force of about 800 men were broken up and militarily defeated while the houses were destroyed and burnt down. There were notes here of some army casualties. It's of note that in the very first paragraph, it says, "The Serbian army units and commands (six brigade)," I think it's a typo. It's actually 6th Brigade. It means Colonel Basara's brigade in Sanski Most. "Territorial Defence units and the SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most area." So it seems it was a joint operation with the 6th Brigade and the TO and the police. The report then talks on about that people arrested were brought in, and it lists some of the weapons at the end of the document that they recovered. Again, I think the document's important because it shows this joint -- the issue of joint operations. It shows that the disarmament plans that were being discussed in the early and middle parts of May were implemented. It highlights to me that a large number of people were captured very quickly. Here they're called civilians, 2.000 of them, and that the operations were over very quickly, and there are references to some Serb casualties. But they didn't seem to be able to take under control large numbers of weapons, let alone any heavy weapons, or other types of activity. So I do know that after this, there were a large number of people, prisoners were taken from Sanski Most and ended up in Manjaca camp. So these are some of the points that I draw from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that, Your Honour, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have D01921, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is another MUP document, another report looking back in part on the disarmament operations. It's cited at footnotes 256, 451, 459, 464, and 566 of your report, so quite heavily cited. It is an exhibit already, but you clearly found this to be an important document for your report. So if you could just take us through it quickly and explain the significance from your perspective to us.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another one of the summary documents I thought was quite useful in explaining what seemed to have happened in Bosanski Novi municipality in May. It highlights a number of the issues we've been talking about so far. It talks at the first part that there was a disarmament operation being planned pursuant to a decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the 16th of April and on the decision of the Government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in association with the Bosanski Novi municipality TO headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop one moment. Just for the record, is that the Subotic order, decision?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, yes. The 16th is the Subotic order. The reference to the ARK decision is probably the early May ARK decision about disarming those in possession of illegally held weapons. There was a plan being drawn up for the confiscation of arms, ammunition, and explosives. And this plan anticipated activities being completed by the 11th of May. And then there is an incident or an operation around 11th of May and then further activity later in that month. And it's clear from this document that as a result of that, large numbers of people were rounded up. And later in the report it talks about them being held in the sports centre and then also some being taken away -- a large number being taken away in trucks, cattle trucks, although some did return. The incident in relation to the cattle trucks is referenced on page 2, where it makes mention that on the 9th of June, members of the municipal staff, of the TO and the military police assembled a railway train made up of 22 closed-type wagons, into which about 4.000 inhabitants from Blagaj Japra, which was the area that the operation had happened in and around -- starting on the 11th of May, which is probably the incident that Mr. Vjestica was talking about at the Assembly session. These individuals from Blagaj Japra were taken to Doboj and I think a couple of days later about 700 of them returned. The document also makes mention in paragraph 2 from page 2 about the resettlement of citizens from Bosanski Novi --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, at -- this would now be page 3 of the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I take you to page 4 of the English version, it makes reference to: "Guided by the decision on the voluntarily resettlement of citizens taken by the Government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the order of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi municipality on the criteria of voluntarily resettlement, Bosanski Novi public security station, at the request of citizens and according to the regulation procedure, performed the following ..." And it talks about the permanently deregistered individuals, 5.680, and other certificates. And this would presumably be relating to the ARK decision that we referenced earlier on the 29th of May. So -- and this document is dated the middle of June, I believe -- I'd have to check, but -- or maybe it's August. It seems clear that Bosanski Novi, there were operations which were formed on the basis of the instructions we've seen before about mobilisation and disarming, that these plans were implemented, that there may have been incidents in the municipality as a result of those operations, but that large numbers of individuals in Bosanski Novi were rounded up and transported out of the municipality, and that also the decision on the deregistering of individuals in Bosanski Novi was implemented and that a large number of people were -- were -- left the area. It says that there were around 7.000 on the transportation on the 9th of -- sorry, 4.000 on the transportation on the 9th of June, of which 700 returned. And then there is also a reference that they were deregistering formally -- the formal process 5.600. So a large number of people in that municipality seemed to have left in a relatively short space of time. And I think it's important because it shows, at least to me, that their -- these documents about establishing plans, establishing plans of disarmament, taking control of territory, and the ultimate end state was that a large number of people in Bosanski Novi were no longer living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move ahead now a little bit, and there is more of this in your report but I'll move ahead past the issue of disarmament now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I would like to bring up 10722, please, it's a 65 ter number. Your Honours, this is cited in footnotes 434, 499, 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's relevant to pages 88 to 97 and paragraphs 2.77 to 2.98 of your report, Mr. Brown. That's a section entitled: "Retaliatory actions and killing of non-Serbs." And can you please just take a look at this document on 3rd September and explain why you selected it. And take your -- take your time to have a look through it if you need to.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's quite a long and detailed report and there are a number of issues that it deals with, including the issues of camps, issues of -- strategic goal, for example, that they had achieved the corridor, the issue of paramilitaries is in there. It's quite a detailed report. Do you want me to highlight some issues that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if I just go through it in order. This is another one of the combat reports that summarises the situation, looks back a little bit in the previous month. In the second paragraph there's a reference to the corps securing the corridor, strategic goal number two. It notes, also on page one, war was prevented from spreading to sensitive areas such as Banja Luka, Prnjavor, Laktasi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and surrounding Banja Luka and other places where the Muslim and Croatian population is dominant. It seems to be that they want to control those areas, irrespective of whether a non-Serb population were in a majority or not. On page 2 there is a reference at the top: "All units and armed formations have essentially been put under control of the 1st Krajina Corps, although there is still resistance from CSB centre." I think this is in relation to the whole issue of paramilitaries and establishing control over paramilitaries by integrating them into the VRS, and this reference may be in relation to a CSB special unit that had operated in Kotor Varos in July and early August and an attempt to try and control that by eventually bringing it into the -- under the -- into the military, integrating it into the military, and whether there was still some resistance from the CSB to do that. Later on down that same page, there is an interesting reference about road building on Manjaca and the reconstruction starting on a church in Sljivno. I think some of the prisoners from Manjaca were used to build that church. At the bottom on page 2 there's references to detention centres and camps. It says: "The intolerant attitude of the international community towards the Serbs' position in BH is causing extreme distrust of their goodwill. In this period, there was great interest in visits to LRZs," which are prisoner of war camps, "with euphoria the dominant feeling, interest in the sick and difficult cases and attempts to show the world the unbearable conditions in those camps." It goes on: "These and especially their negative portrayal of the situation has increased the antagonism of soldiers towards the international institutions. We were confronted with the problem of having to refuse their visits to many check-points because of this."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we go to page 3 of the English now, which is also page 3 of the original.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The most evident example was the calculated, tactless, and unannounced visit by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Although the majority of foreign journalists portrayed the situation very realistically, both on the battle-field and in the camps controlled by us, some journalists especially from Canada used skilful fabrications to try and blame the Serbs and the FRY for the crisis." Mr. Mazowiecki had visited Manjaca camp not long before this report was written, but he had been denied entry. There's a reference a little bit down that paragraph: "Mr. Karadzic's statement that he will concede 20 per cent of the territory controlled by the SR army to the enemies in order to achieve a peaceful solution caused some bitterness and a drop in motivation. Blood was shed and many lives were lost for these territories, so it is impossible to convince soldiers that this is a diplomatic move." This may be of some note because at the 16th Assembly Session there were a number of delegates who were articulating or advocating that they should be controlling significant territories, and Mr. Karadzic, I believe, and others were more cautious to say: We shouldn't be controlling everything. We just should be controlling the territories we want to all intents and purposes. It may very well be that Mr. Karadzic was indicating here that they were willing to cede certain territories back in order to achieve a peaceful solution, but there were some individuals. I know some people were talking about areas, for example, even Tuzla and some of the areas elsewhere in Bosnia that they felt they should control. Maybe Mr. Karadzic and others felt it more realistic to control the territories they could control rather than the ones they wanted to. Or maybe there was a realisation that they could afford to trade off some territories and that this wasn't going down well with the soldiers on the ground who had, in essence, fought for those and died for those areas. Jajce, for example, was not a municipality or an area that was historically Serb, but the VRS did take it and maybe there was negotiations that certain areas could be traded back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you stated that you believe Mr. Karadzic and others were more cautious to say, in terms of the territories, and further you said: "Maybe Mr. Karadzic and others felt it more realistic to control the territories they could control rather than the ones that they wanted to." What's the basis for you to reach such conclusion and how it -- does it relate to your military expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think reading the Assembly -- 16th Assembly Session in particular, there may also be some references in the Mladic diary, I'd have to go back over them, but a number of delegates at the 16th Assembly Session were very much advocating territory, maybe even territories that they themselves came from, that they should control. I remember, at least off the top of my head, one delegate talking about: We should have Tuzla or an area close to Tuzla. I think Mr. Karadzic and others were more -- were more of the line of: We need to define the territories we want, not necessarily the territories -- all the territories we can get. And it's clear -- for example, I mention Jajce. It was predominantly a Croat municipality. It was also -- there was a strategic interest because there was a hydro-electric plant that supplied electricity throughout Bosnia. But the Serbs -- the Serb army captured Jajce. They also captured some of the municipalities in the corridor which were Croat predominantly. And they were quite successful, certainly in the Krajina area militarily, they seized a lot of territory. But it may not have been the territory that they felt they -- that they often called it their territory, our hearts and language like that, but that it would have been beneficial to have it in order to have it traded back at some negotiation. That was my -- and that was my interpretation of some of the comments from the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but I didn't hear an answer to the second part of your question which is what expertise does he have to read the minutes of the Assembly and give us his interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we've gone through that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's for us to assess later on. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, and then if we could just -- any other sections of this document that you'd like to point out before we move on?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on -- keeping on page 3, there's a reference: "The ICR's approach to distributing humanitarian aid is having a very detrimental effect on the morale of soldiers and units. This aid is mostly distributed to prisoners of war, Muslims, Croats, and crisis areas." And they seem to say here that there hasn't been a case of aid, in essence, being given to threatened Serbs. In paragraph 2 at the bottom of this page, there's a reference to paramilitary governments and armed formations, this issue of paramilitaries, increasing extremism towards Muslim and Croat population continues -- but there are continued efforts to place the organs of authority and the MUP above military formations. So here are some of the problems that the 1st Krajina Corps can see. Adverse situations regarding power supply and distribution of supplies. And for this reason, the 1st Krajina Corps commander held a meeting with unit commanders and municipal presidents at which he pointed to the problem of the existence of paragovernments and paramilitaries and the need to overcome this crisis, the involvement of civilians or paramilitaries outside the control were identified by the 1st Krajina Corps as a problem. And here it would seem that General Talic in an attempting to resolve those issues is getting together unit and brigade commanders and municipal civilian leaders in order to try and thrash out and come to an agreement how to resolve this issue. It notes: "There are -- certain tensions are still present in Kotor Varos, Kljuc, and Sanski Most areas because a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion." The corps seems to think they've got evidence that many people who have been arrested -- there's no evidence that they've done anything wrong, and this is echoed, certainly in some of the Manjaca camp documents that I saw after I'd written this report, that a -- quite a large number or a number of the individuals who had been brought to Manjaca, there was no evidence that they had been involved in armed rebellion, there was no -- they weren't carrying weapons, they weren't in uniform. And to all intents and purposes, this gives me the impression along with other documents, not only that the corps aware that there was a large number of people who weren't involved in armed rebellion, but they were still arrested. There's a reference the CSB, especially from Prijedor -- this is on to page 4. "... is not contributing to this approach. Prijedor, headed by Stevo Drljaca, who led a convoy of people who wanted to leave the crisis area - they committed a massacre on the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men who wanted to leave the territory of the Krajina autonomous region." This is relating to an incident on Vlasic mountain where a convoy of people had been transported to Travnik, people were taken out and killed. This was reported in the 1st Krajina Corps documents, by the way, in daily combat reports, which went up to the Main Staff at the time, but this is a summary of what had happened. "This action caused indignation not only among citizens but also among 1st Krajina Corps soldiers. This dark stain which was created did not have support, but it is very fortunate that the international community did not find out about it in more detail." The 1st Krajina Corps knew about it very quickly because they reported the incidents in their daily combat report, but it seems to be here that they seem more -- or at least they're making reference to the fact that they're fortunate that the international community didn't get to hear about it, presumably it would have caused them significant problems if they had. There's also a reference in the next paragraph: "In Celinac area, soldiers on leave took reprisals because of the activities of Muslims and Ustasha forces in the Vevcani village area." It's not clear what the reprisals are, but there are one or two references in the Krajina Corps document collections about reprisals, including one large incident in Vecici in Kotor Varos in November -- early November 1992, in which a large number of individuals are reported as being massacred after being captured. And there are a smaller number of references in the Krajina Corps documents of reprisals, including killings, that occur. Those are I think -- I know it's a long document and maybe I've answered your question in a rather large -- long way, but these are some of the points that I've brought out from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, thank you. That does lead us to essentially my last topic, which is camps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe it's already admitted unless I -- no -- yes, Your Honour, I do tender that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You cover Manjaca camp quite -- quite heavily in your report, and you talk in paragraph 2.133 of the report in summary about how the camps in your view in essence - I'll use your words - became part of the planned expulsion of non-Serbs from the area. They're a component of the policy of separation. So that is the part I will -- we will be talking about next. Mr. Brown, there's been quite a lot of evidence on Manjaca presented, so I'll go through this part quite quickly. Just before we take the break, instead of going through the documents, you've already alluded to that there were reports indicating that the 1KK knew about mistreatment of prisoners or that prisoners were in Manjaca who had not -- there was not evidence that they had participated in the armed rebellion. If you could just --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we should take the break now, Your Honour, I don't think I can get through this in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm going to skip ahead a little bit now in the interests of time. On page 29 of the transcript today, discussing P3929, that's the 1KK -- the large 1KK morale report of 3rd September, in your answer you noted that Mr. Mazowiecki had recently been denied access to Manjaca when discussing that 3rd September report. I'd like to bring up 65 ter 01614, please. This is a 1KK command report signed by -- again, by the assistant commander for morale, Colonel Vukelic, dated 23rd of August, 1992. And I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, this report is cited at footnotes 187, 494, and footnote 752 and discussed on page 105 of the report in connection with Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Although it is listed -- the footnotes were listed in your notice, but it's very difficult to locate it at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I should say, Your Honours, and I'll discuss this with my friend, but we do have a hyperlinked chart of all the footnotes with 65 ter numbers which makes it -- which we've provided to the Defence which makes it easier to look things up. So that's something we could talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But could you just take a look at this report, Mr. Brown, and I think this is the one you were referring to, and tell us about the significance of this document and Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this seems to give just some more details to the Mazowiecki visit, which, according to the document at least, was at the proposal of the Banja Luka mayor. He visits or tries to visit the camp but is denied. And maybe some of the comments in the document are of note. It states that he was concerned whether human rights are being respected and expressed his wish to visit the detention camp at Manjaca presumably in his capacity as a UN human rights representative. He was informed of the struggle of the people of the Serbian Republic, the difficulties arising from the blockades by the international community, obstructions in receiving aid and threats of military intervention. He, Mr. Mazowiecki, then seemed to reply that he'd come on a humanitarian visit but the report says he failed to demonstrate his intentions. Instead he wanted to visit and inspect the detention camp. Asked about the purpose for his visit, he replied, The respect for human rights. The document then says: Asked to reply whose rights he was inspecting, he said the rights of the prisoners. He was given a detailed account of the Manjaca prisoner of war camp and advised that he should also respect the rights of the Serbian people. In response he did not react or show any interest in this remark. It's noted that -- he said he was asked under whose authority he had come on a goodwill mission and he replied that he had been so charged by the legal BH government. He was warned that only the government of the Serbian Republic could approve this and without such approval he was not allowed to talk to anyone or visit the prisoner of war camp. And he clearly was denied access to the camp. On page 2 there's a reference to a confidential order which I'm not clear about, but: "We prevented them from going to the camp on the pretext that they did not have permission from the Serbian Republic government. "According to Mr. Radic said that he had spoken with Minister Buha, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Karadzic about the visit. In a telephone conversation, they agreed to meet with the delegation, but suggested leaving the final decision to the military authorities. For this reason, please co-ordinate such activities in the future in order to avoid them running counter to your orders." So clearly he was refused entry. And the last paragraph is of note. It states: "Regardless of the consequences of the cancellation of Mr. Mazowiecki's visit to the prisoner of war camp, we declare with full responsibility that the purpose of his visit was not inspecting the state of human rights, but on the contrary, intelligence, reconnaissance, which can be confirmed by those representatives of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina who were present and who spoke with him." So it would seem that the military refused his visit and believed that Mr. Mazowiecki wasn't there with the purpose of inspecting the human rights of the prisoners, but on some kind of intelligence or reconnaissance task. Bearing in mind that the ICRC had visited the camp in July previously, and there are documents in the Krajina Corps collection on that visit which indicate that the camp was in a poor condition or at least some of the prisoners were in a poor condition and there was notification of blood trails and mistreatment of prisoners, so this visit comes about a month after that, but clearly that he is denied access and sent away. And the implication in the document is that he's not there on a genuine mission to inspect the rights of prisoners but on some other ulterior motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Brown, the documents you refer to which show some of the evidence of mistreatment and knowledge of mistreatment of prisoners and poor conditions I'm not going to go over now. I'm now going to move to 65 ter 04225, relatively late in the year 1KK command report, a regular combat report, dated 16 December 1992. And I'd like you to tell us about this document and how it's significant. It's footnoted at footnotes 513 and 518 of your report which are on pages 108 and 104 of the report -- 108 and 109, excuse me, of the report where you discuss this document. And keeping in mind what I had started to raise earlier, the analysis you put forth in 2.1333 of your report about the link between camps and removal of the population.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document seems to be one of the -- if you like, the end documents in relation to Manjaca in 1992 and what happened to those prisoners who were held there. Many of them had been captured in June or at least taken to Manjaca in June and July. There are visits of -- many of them had arrived at Manjaca from other camps, mainly in -- from Omarska, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, although there are reference of other places. So many of the prisoners had been taken to Manjaca from other detention centres. Through the summer there are references which are noted in the report and also subsequent documents that many of the prisoners did not deserve to be there, references in their own report that I've talked about before. The conditions were poor, noted in ICRC visit and also in their own Manjaca documents. The camp itself was a series of cattle sheds on a military farm, a former military farm. The prisoners were held there until the end of the year. There are reports in the documents of a lack of water, the water-pipes couldn't supply the camps. There are references in one or two documents about the cold conditions later in the year. The prisoners were -- there are documentary references of the prisoners undertaking work, some of which which may even be of a military nature in support of engineering units. There was a release of some 700 prisoners in November. I think around 3.000 was the maximum number of prisoners in Manjaca. There was a release in November, but a large number of them, about 2.000 of them, stayed there until December. And they were released in two batches, one on this day and I believe another thousand two days previously. But it seems to me -- and they were released from Manjaca not back to their homes, not back to their municipalities, but were escorted in convoys over into Croatia and released. And when I looked at that sequence of events and being aware that there were convoys of individuals leaving Trnopolje, leaving Omarska, that in relation to many of the people who were held in detention that the camps were a means or a part of the process by which people were removed from the territory. It's not maybe the only one, we've talked about the deregistration process, but it seems that Manjaca was linked very much to other camps. It involved the operation of the military, also included interrogations in the movement and use of the police to bring people there. And -- but at the end of the day, the prisoners in Manjaca were not returned home but they were escorted out of RS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we see that in paragraph 3; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 3 says: "One thousand and one prisoners were released today from Manjaca camp - they were escorted out of the RS ... 413 of them still remain scheduled to be released on Friday ... there have been no other significant changes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P3931.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, redacted version will be -- his -- I mean his report will be tendered? Has it been already tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe I did tender it and it was admitted, Your Honours, at the beginning of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you thinking of the CV or -- I think he was referring to the redacted version of the report with the paragraphs deleted that were ordered to be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, I -- no, Your Honour, we will tender that. I didn't know whether you wanted a redacted version or you would just skip those sections in your review, but we can redact those parts and submit it. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think in terms of CV we admitted both versions, one under seal and one publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given the time that we have and the sheer size of your report, with a large number of paragraphs and footnotes, I'll strive to put as simple questions as possible which could hopefully be answered with a yes or a no. Of course, you are free to expand whenever you deem necessary. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I'd like us to look at your relationship with the Prosecution. You worked for the OTP between 1998 and 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your job as part of the Prosecution developed in a way. Did it at all times include the investigative part as well as analysis or did these two things come one after another?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job within the OTP was as a military analyst. The role within the military analysis team -- the role of the military analyst was to provide analytical support to the investigative teams, and that usually comprised of a number of tasks. Reviewing documents was a key task and providing documentary references to the investigative teams. But there were times in the investigation process where I was expected to assist them in the -- their own function and also to assist the trial attorneys understand the context or understand certain documentations that were in the possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 1D4848.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which is your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case. E-court it is page 192 and 193. While we wait for it I wanted to tell you this. They asked you whether you were employed as a military analyst and you responded with a "yes." Next you were asked about your participation in investigating measures undertaken by the Prosecution, the OTP, that is to say. You said that it was correct. And then you were asked whether it was true that you interviewed witnesses for the needs of the Prosecution. Could you tell us whether you, indeed, interviewed witnesses on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in a number of interviews, as directed by the investigation team. They were relatively small in number and they usually involved military figures in which the investigation team wanted to use documentation that would help them and also where my expertise, based on the analysis of military documents, could help in that interview process. So yes, I did take part in a number of interviews; they were relatively small in number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to witness interviews, did you also take part in interviewing potential suspects?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the same -- generally the same interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender these two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt and I'm sorry. I'm just not sure of the point of tendering pages where the witness says he took parts in interviews, where the witness has just said on the record in our case: I took part in interviews. Exactly the same thing, I believe, as what is being tendered so -- no objection, but I don't really see the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, I see your point, Mr. Nicholls. Do we really need to admit this, given the admission of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it is enough to have the transcript page recorded in our transcript; however, we'll have a number of pages that we will refer to from this testimony and others. I believe it might be easier for the Bench to simply admit these two pages and the other pages that I will be referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us leave it at that. We'll give the number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you interview, for example, Colonel Basara, Branko Basara? You mentioned him today.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I took part in that interview. I wasn't the only one, I wasn't leading the interview, but I took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Basara was to -- was supposed to appear as a witness in this case as well?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 194 admitted from the same document, 1D4848, lines 6, 7, and 8. Perhaps it could be joined with the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the point. Did we see the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's not necessary, perhaps. The witness confirmed it was so and that is where we find that piece of information, that he interviewed Branko Basara, commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Could we have page 15 -- 195, but it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you also interview the person in question - I won't mention the name in open session, it was a protected witness. Please have a look at the name in line 11.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I did take part in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the second box contains an answer of yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second box appears to have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the answer begins with line 19; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this page be added as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done, but for the ease of reference you just first put the question and if witness confirms we move on. Consult Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we would have had to move into private session to do that and perhaps that's a better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That -- just a second. That will be admitted -- added under seal that part so -- but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So far the admit -- those parts admitted were dealt with in private session in previous case so Exhibit P3932 will be put under seal, but in the future I would rather put your question directly in this trial without having to refer to the previous testimony. If witness confirms, that's it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe it would be a better way to go about it, but then I would have to spend more time in explaining the circumstances my question refers to. Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, did you take part in investigations concerning persons against whom you later testified?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure quite what you mean by taking part in investigations. An investigation a quite a wide-encompassing phrase. I took part in work for the OTP on cases that did end up with accused and from which I testified. So, for example, the Brdjanin -- Mr. Brdjanin's case -- my work was slightly different in the OTP -- or at least the work of the analysis, in that we tended to support a number of cases, mainly because of the nature of the work we were doing and the material we were reviewing which Prosecutors believed was useful for multiple cases. So in that regard, I took part in working on cases which, in a number of cases, did lead to an accused appearing here and for which I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 196 of this document - it needn't be uploaded - in lines 16 and 17 you said: [In English] "So we worked -- clearly we worked closely with the investigating team."
