[Interpretation] Et cetera. I'm interested in this: You participated in the work of the investigations team and what you said just now was said in open session, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 22651, page 428 in e-court. Let's look at pages 17 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed again that you had worked as part of the investigation section.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a member of the investigation team. I was a member of the military analysis team. The military analysis team supported a number of investigation teams as well as supporting the senior trial attorneys, to whom their -- the analysts' work was useful. So I'm not sure what your question is, Mr. Karadzic, in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In terms of organigram, military analysis team belongs to investigating team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two analysis teams in the Office of the Prosecutor: Military analysis team and the leadership research team. Each team had a number of professional analysts within it. There were a number of investigation teams which had one or a number of cases. The analysts in the LRT and the MAT supported those investigation teams --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is the immediate supervisor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My immediate supervisor was the head of the military analysis team, not the head of the investigation team. And my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And head of the analysis team is supervised by who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The head of investigations, chief of investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although it did change and then I think chief of prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, no -- no objection. Sorry to interrupt. But if we continue with Mr. Karadzic citing to pages of previous transcripts, no problem at all. But I see that what Mr. Karadzic is doing is giving page numbers of a document that he is using which do not correspond to the transcript pages. The conventional way of citing to a previous case is to cite the transcript pages. In this case it's - my eyes aren't good enough - 21491 that we're talking about. It's just a suggestion because it would make the record clearer and easier to follow in the future rather than having to have the exhibits at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably he was referring to the e-court number, but I would appreciate he would also cite the transcript page as well. But before that, I just doubt the necessity of relying on those transcripts. He can put his question directly and he dealt with his involvement in the investigation as a whole in his examination-in-chief. Well, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as pages are concerned, I believe it's easier for the officer to find it if I give the page number in e-court. That's why I did it that way. As for displaying, I have to do it this way because the witness just asked me what I mean. I'm interested in lines 24 and 25. I want to know if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were part of investigations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was part of the investigation division. I was not part of the investigation teams within that division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it's necessary. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In how many cases -- never mind. You were part of that division all the time, the investigation division; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on page 61, the distinguished Mr. Nicholls asked you why you had chosen that document. So you were selecting documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On what criteria?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, first of all what I did was I would review the documents in chronological order and clearly when I had realised myself what I wanted my report and the shape of my report to be, if there were documents that I thought were useful to explain a particular theme, I would include them in those -- in those -- in that section. But I was the one who organised the report and reviewed the material and selected documents I thought talked to those themes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You selected documents that supported the indictment; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, Mr. Karadzic. I was not working on this particular case. I was writing a report in relation to operations in the Krajina. I did not know what the indictment was for this case, so I didn't write the report in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did appraise the usefulness of documents; that's what you just said a moment ago. From what viewpoint did you do that, usefulness for what?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usefulness in understanding the operations in the Krajina in the time-period that I was looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you then put together the whole truth about operations in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already highlighted yesterday the limitations of the report and I make no bones that this is not a report that covers every single aspect of operations in the Krajina. I'm not sure what you mean by "the whole truth." This report was based on military -- contemporaneous military documents and other contemporary documents predominantly from a collection that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor and it is sourced predominantly by that type of material, and I've tried to be as objective as I can in what these documents tell me. But I'm more than happy to say to the Court, as I've already done, that there are limitations within the documents, limitations within the sources, and therefore there will be limitations of the report. But I've tried to be as objective as I can based on the sources and the material that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the OTP was in possession of a certain number of documents. Who made the selection of documents that would become part of your report eventually?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in assuming that you did that by reviewing everything and then selecting some?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you do with documents that seem favourable to the Serbian side, the 1st Krajina Corps, and even the Serbian policies? What did you do with documents that fall under Rule 68? Were they incorporated in your report too?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I had -- I knew my obligation under Rule 68, and when I had documents that I thought might look -- fall into that category, I raised that and flagged that to the trial attorneys in -- in the OTP. I'm not sure what you mean by documents that seem favourable to the Serbian side. I think there are many documents in this report in certain categories that talk about, for example, casualties that the Serbs took. There are references to areas that, for example, in the Croat corridor where the Croats were -- had armed militarily and taken over territory there. There is documents in relation to paramilitaries, for example. So I'm not sure what you mean by look favourable on the side of the Serbs, but I was aware of my obligations and any documents that I felt could fall in that I raised to the appropriate trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you incorporate them in your report and draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to them? Do we find in your footnotes documents that fall under Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I included in some of the categories I've talked about there areas that may potentially seem Rule 68, but I'm not a lawyer. I know my obligation and I included the documents that I thought were relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we could say that the documents disclosed to us by the OTP under Rule 68 as potentially exculpatory are also to be found in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's really a question for the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness referred to Rule 68 documents and I think Mr. Karadzic is asking whether those documents are reflected in his report. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand that. I'm just not sure that Mr. Brown would be in a position to know what at the time of his report the complete Rule 68 disclosure was. He said that he's -- I'll leave it. It's just a -- it may be beyond the scope of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the witness is able to answer the question. Mr. Brown -- just a second. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] -- provide them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Rule 68 documents have been provided by the Office of the Prosecutor in this case at all. That's -- all I can say is that when I reviewed documents, I looked at them, and if there was any that I thought potentially were Rule 68, then I flagged them up at the time. I can't remember specific documents, but I do know that there were some areas in the report that may go to certain issues. For example, the Serbs taking casualties. There were some areas that were armed in the municipalities, the actions of Croats in municipalities in corridor -- municipalities in -- these type of things and I include it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us now forget about Rule 68. The documents that you pointed out to the Prosecution as documents that are potentially exculpatory as far as the 1st Krajina Corps and the Serbian politicians are concerned, are they to be found in your report and in your footnotes or did you just tell the OTP that such documents exist?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in the categories I've talked about I think there are references in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you've included all such documents, all the documents that you told the Prosecution were favourable to the Serbian side. Did you include each one of them and provided your comment on them?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my understanding that Rule 68 was one that was to provide material favourable to the Serbian side. It's my understanding - and I would have to read Rule 68 again, it was a long time since I've worked here - but that it went to the potential guilt or innocence of an accused. I don't remember too many documents that fell under that category when I was writing the report. The report at the time became, after I started writing it, became more interesting to the Talic case, General Talic/Brdjanin case. And I raised any concerns I had and documents in that case. But I -- it wasn't my understanding that it was about providing material that's favourable to the Serbian side. As I said, there were materials in there that undoubtedly portrayed some of the problems that the Serbs faced. And I've included those in the report in order to be as objective as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to put to you the following. You were working for the Office of the Prosecutor in an effort to support the indictment, and that's how you selected your documents. If you came across a document that did not support the indictment, you reported that to the OTP; but you did not include such documents, at least not all such documents in your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you disagree, then that should mean we can find those documents in your report in the footnotes accompanied with your comment.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've explained, Mr. Karadzic, my position in relation to Rule 68 when I was writing the report in 2002 and before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it can't be that you only reported them to the Prosecution and included some of them. What was your relationship exactly with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think that has been asked and answered. Let's move on to specific topics. And further, witness denied that he worked at the OTP in an effort to support the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On two pages in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, pages 199 and 200, the witness says a lot about that and I would like to include these two pages in evidence with the previous exhibit number, the first six lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. If you would like to tender that, you show that and then ask the witness about it. I'm just -- I'm doubting whether it is really necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid it is, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then put your question. Let's upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D4848, page 199. That's in e-court. It's the right page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first seven lines. You were asked about this report from 2002; correct? Can you see the first seven lines?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your answer is that you sent your analysis to the party that had requested it; right? That's line 10. And then in line 17, you answered that the requesting party would come back to you with some feedback in terms of additional requests or additional clarifications and you provided them; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In summary, I wrote the report and completed it. There was a process of some peer review internally within the military analysis team, and then once I was happy with that process it was -- it was disseminated to the interested party, who would read it, who read it, and came back with any -- if it needed any clarification. But as I recall, I don't think there were any -- too many changes at all. And, if anything, it was cosmetic presentational issues or spelling issues. But I don't remember any substantive changes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But anyway, the requesting party had the possibility to put their objections or comments or additional requests, and that made you revise your report or supplement it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have any substantive comments, and if they had wanted me to change the report, I would have had to look at that quite significantly and decide whether -- whether that was the case. But in reality, they didn't. I wouldn't just change the report because somebody else within the OTP wanted me to change it. I wouldn't have done that and I didn't do that anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in lines 17 through 20 we see that it was indeed so. You say there were not many such requests, but that existed as a possibility and did happen to some extent. Doesn't your answer indicate that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there -- the sort of comments they might have -- it was a long time ago, but the comments I believe they had was a presentational one. It wasn't anything to do with substance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please, the first six lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this correct? You accepted the claim, the assertion, made in this question; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I think that was true. I believe that that was the case. And there was some alterations I made subsequent to testimony. I put some errata in and some -- a change more recently. But there was -- this was not a report that the Office of the Prosecutor were asking me to amend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, 201, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here you speak about the limitations, and you say there were time limitations, language limitations, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these two pages be added?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask Mr. Robinson to give his observation as to the usefulness or necessity or -- I don't see much difference from what he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that it's better if Dr. Karadzic puts his question to the witness and only refers to the transcript if the answer is inconsistent with what was said in the transcript. Other than that, I think it's better to just put the assertion directly to the witness and only resort to the transcript in the event of an inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please heed to that advice. I don't see the necessity to receive these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the other point, Dr. Karadzic, is it simply quadruples the time that you take, and when time is of the essence, it's not an efficient way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My intention is to establish the capacity of this witness, whether he is really an expert who in an unbiased and scientific way wrote his report, or is it, in fact, evidence given by a member of the OTP team. And then I should ask Mr. Robinson to give evidence for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a totally unnecessary and unacceptable statement on your part. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed in the Brdjanin case that you had selected documents together with your colleagues from the team - just a moment - and that you were familiar with the indictment; right? You had learned the indictment previously?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Brdjanin case I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that we recognise the language of the indictment in your report and vice versa, tell me, please, did you write your report after 2002? You made it after at least two indictments were brought against me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was completed on the date that it's noted, which I think is November -- I think there were two drafts, one a few months prior to that, November 2002, and I'd actually been working on the report for a long time. This wasn't the only thing I was doing in the -- obviously the process of going through the documents and others was quite time-consuming. But I'm not sure what your point is about it was written after at least two indictments were brought against me. I don't know if you can explain that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So were you aware of the indictments that were issued against me when you started working on this report? And generally speaking indictments against Serbs containing certain assertions that are repeated in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of an indictment or maybe more indictments I don't -- against you. I don't believe I read them. I wasn't working in support at that time of the team that was working on this case. So your indictment did not form the basis of this report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is what I'm interested in. In the report and during the examination-in-chief you made an assertion, stating that what the Serbs wanted during the separation process -- to remove Croats and Muslims from territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina that they thought they were entitled to. Now, please help us with this: Was that incorporated into the indictment as taken from your report or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I have no idea about the issue of the compilation of the indictment against you. I was aware of indictment, maybe even indictments, if they were amended, against you. I wasn't working in relation to that. I was working in relation to providing a report. How others may have used sections of the report, I don't know. But the report was written in an -- at least initially in an attempt for me to understand and exploit a source of documents that the OTP had in their possession. When it became clear that this might be relevant in the Brdjanin/Talic case, Ms. Korner asked me to compile a report. I took that away. I laid down the scope of the report, utilising the documents at my disposal, and I provided the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Brdjanin case, right, you spoke about what your share was in writing the indictments and you said that you were asked for comments during the indictment process, as it were, and that you provided your own contribution in this way to the writing of indictments; right? I mean you did not write them up because you were not a lawyer, but you did take part with your own suggestions and comments that you were asked to provide; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've been -- I am not objecting. I'd like a cite at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have to waste time. 65 ter 22651 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is not a waste of time to conduct a cross-examination properly, which is to cite the witness's prior statements to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. If you cite, you have to cite correctly. But let us see the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I recounted it. 65 ter 22651, page 21490 or 247 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this. You were asked here about the content of the indictment. You said -- further down, from line 11 onwards, the question ends in the following way: "Did you assist in any way in drafting the indictment?" And then your explanation is that you did that if you were asked to provide your comments, right? This goes all the way down to line 17.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with what I've said there. I didn't draft the indictment, it wasn't my function, but lawyers at some stage would come and say did I have any comments on this particular issue or could I have support, was there any documents that might speak to this particular aspect. But it wasn't my job to write the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was the only way in which you participated in creating the indictment, when you were just asked to support something you would find a document or you would give your comment; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others created the indictment, others were working on the indictment, and they may have come and said: What do you think about this? Is there any documentation that might help you? I didn't write the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In how many cases -- for how many indictments did they ask for your opinion or for documents that would support the indictment? Up until 2004, how many? Each and every one?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not each and every one. I know that in the Talic/Brdjanin one there was requests. I believe in the Stakic case it had already been written. I wasn't involved in the Stanisic/Zupljanin indictment. And I can't remember about Mr. Krajisnik. It may well have been -- I'd have to check the timings. It may well be that they asked for advice, but I can't remember about the issue of the indictment for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not in this case, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in this case, Your Honour, no. I have not had anything to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they seek your advice in respect of indictments, again [as interpreted] Muslim generals, Delic, Halilovic, and other commanders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in those cases. It may have been that some of my analyst colleagues might ask me for some documents or assistance who were involved in those cases, but I wasn't involved at all so I wasn't asked in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who worked on those cases? Who was your counterpart in those cases?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember which of my colleagues. I know there are a number -- a couple of colleagues who were working on ABiH cases, but I can't remember what the division of their labour was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any such report, an expert report of theirs on the behaviour of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if they wrote reports or not. I can't remember. It wasn't the focus of my work particularly, so I'm not sure. I know that -- well, I -- I was going to say I believe some may have testified, but I don't even want to say that because I can't remember. It was some time ago. But there were colleagues working on those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you have not found a report akin to yours, that had to do with the BH army I mean, and you don't know whether any such report exists?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't know, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you saying that in assessing the behaviour of the 1st Krajina Corps, it was of no relevance to you whatsoever how the other side was behaving, the party fighting against the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not of no relevance. It was of relevance and there are references in the Krajina Corps' own documents that make reference to the activities of the ABiH. I don't doubt that in certain areas the Krajina Corps was conducting some quite tough fighting against the ABiH and elsewhere. I don't doubt that in even some of the municipality attacks that the 1st Krajina Corps forces took some casualties. I state that in the report. So it's not of no relevance, but I was utilising the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps, and it makes reference to activities of the ABiH which I -- in some areas I don't doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you had no insight into my indictment, does that mean that this particular wording that I believe is the very foundation of the indictment against me, the only link, the only incrimination that has to do with the chaos of the civil war and my intentions, stating that we wanted to separate from the Muslims who lived in our area, is that something that you established if you did not take over from the indictment against me? The wording is identical, and did you establish that independently of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the writing of the indictment, Mr. Karadzic. I wrote my report based on the documents that I saw. In relation to the issue of separation, I think there are documents in the 1st Krajina Corps and elsewhere that -- having reviewed those documents and reviewed the events that occurred, in particular in May, June, July, August 1992, it was my analysis that separation was a critical feature and that the Bosnian Serbs wished to establish their own state, they wanted to separate from the Muslim and Croat communities, and that also included as a result the removal of non-Serbs from the territory that they wished to control. And I analysed -- reached that conclusion based on the documents in the 1st Krajina Corps and elsewhere. How that links to the indictment is not one I can answer. I was not involved in the drafting of this indictment against you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you conclude that on the basis of what was happening during those months of the war or did you find programmes, decisions, on the basis of which this happened and did that lead you to that conclusion? So was it induction or deduction?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered the question, Mr. Karadzic. Documents such as the 16th Assembly Session, references in the 1st Krajina Corps about separation, the actions and results of operations in May, June, and July identified in many of the 1 Krajina Corps documents led me to the conclusion about this issue of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you mention this in this transcript, did I say at the Assembly that the Drina should not be a boundary between two Serb states or between two worlds?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can have a second to refresh myself on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at page 7 of the transcript as well, the last paragraph in Serbian -- no, no, page 8.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the minutes that I've got here, it states that you articulated at the session: "The third strategic goal is to establish the corridor on the Drina valley, that is, elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. We are on both sides of the Drina and our strategic interests and living space are there. We now see a possibility for some Muslim municipalities to be set up along the Drina as enclaves in order for them to achieve their rights, but that belt along the Drina must basically belong to the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. As much as it is strategically useful for us in a positive way, it helps us by damaging the interests of our enemy in establishing a corridor which would connect them to the Muslim international and render this area permanently unstable."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, what are these two worlds that I'm referring to in relation to the Drina as a boundary? Or more specifically, do you accept that, traditionally, Drina was considered to be the boundary between the East and the West, between Orthodoxy and Catholicism, and that this is repeated in many interviews, documents, discussions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. It's not exactly clear from your statement what that means. It could be read that if it's true that the Drina was seen historically as some boundary between East and West, that by controlling that area, that is, having Serbs on both sides of the Drina, it would no longer be such a boundary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the explanation I provided on Serb TV in 1993, what that strategic objective means? I explained, before Maas tricht at that, that in Europe all the borders are going to be soft, so that should be a soft border too. That is what I explicitly said television. Krajisnik and I gave an interview on television.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you able to show that to me so I could read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I do hope that we will be in a position to put it to you on Tuesday. I'm not prepared to do it now, but this does complete the picture. In response to a question put by a journalist in 1993, what this third strategic objective was, my answer was: All of Europe is going to have soft borders. Izetbegovic agreed that on the Una and the Drina borders should not be needed, and I explained that there would be no border restrictions on that border like, very soon, all of Europe would not have any border restrictions. You didn't know that; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know those comments that you made in 1993. What I do know, at least reading the documents including directive four which was found in the Krajina Corps collection, was that the Drina Corps was tasked with driving out -- destroying the forces -- Muslim forces in the Cerska Valley and forcing the civilian population to leave, that there were documents preceding that of meetings we talked about yesterday, that there were Drina Corps instructions following that, including a meeting, that there were documents from the Drina Corps itself echoing that objective, and operations were put in place in November and December 1992 on the Drina with that objective. And it would -- and that actually went on into the early months of 1993. And it would seem to me from reading those documents and also the articulation at the Assembly session that by that time, in November 1993 [sic], the objectives set before the military were to seize control of the Cerska Valley and the Drina valley in order for the Serbs to take that area, and obviously with Serbia being on the other side, that that land would be controlled by them. And certainly from operational directive four, the inference -- in fact, the stated objective is to cause the civilian population to leave, which would seem to me, again, to indicate that it was not just a case of militarily defeating an armed group in the Drina valley, but that in order to take permanent control of that, individuals, Muslims or non-Serbs, would be driven out and that that's what the objective, set the military at the end of 1993 in the Drina valley, was. But I can't comment on what you may have said publicly in your press statements in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, did you find that Drina Corps document in the Banja Luka collection as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operational directive four was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said -- you referred to a document which Drina Corps issued itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was a document that was shown to me in a statement a couple of years ago, I believe in 2010. There was a series of document seizures, I believe, of the Drina Corps, and although operational directive four was found in the -- which I cite in my report, was found in the Drina Corps collection, I was asked to comment later on on whether those documents added to my understanding of how directives worked. And it seemed to me that it was quite similar to how directive one had been pushed down in June with those issues of preliminary meetings or meetings, directives being sent, instructions being acted upon down at corps level and with subordinate formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic, five minutes before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, it is with great pleasure that we are going to shed more light on this on Tuesday. We are not in a position today, to do so today. You will see that your conclusions are totally wrong and that it's actually the other way around. But please focus on the third objective now. Is it correct that in that Drina River valley that you are speaking about, what is envisaged is that there would be Muslim municipalities in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem from your comment at the 16th Assembly Session, Mr. Karadzic, that at that time you may have countenanced the idea of having some Muslim enclaves in the Drina valley. That does not seem to have been the case come November 1993 -- sorry, 1992, with operational directive four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that. Do you know that in almost all the plans that we accepted, what was envisaged was that there should be Muslims in the Drina River valley even after the fighting for Cerska, that they would be there either as enclaves in Republika Srpska or as part of the Muslim constituent unit. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that and operational directive four doesn't seem to imply that either. Nor -- nor does the Drina Corps' own instruction based on directive four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I put it to you now, Mr. Brown, that the fighting in the Drina valley was not motivated by our ambition for them not to have a municipality, their own municipalities there, but rather motivated by the unbearable shooting at our troops and our people in the back. In 1993 we simply could not take it any longer, to have fighting against us take place in our rear. And even after 1993 we accepted that they would have their own territories there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of all the details in the Drina valley, but I am aware that the Muslim forces in that area conducted operations that I believe did involve destruction of Serbian villages. I do believe that they had a degree of success. Whether operational directive four was based on that in order to stop that, it's not an area that I've looked at in detail. But it would seem to me, irrespective of what had happened and what was going on, that there came a time in November 1992 that the VRS Main Staff pushed out an operational directive, indicating that the Muslim forces in the Cerska Valley were to be driven out along with the civilian population and that that was echoed by a Drina Corps order themselves based on that directive and that they conducted operations in November and December based on that. They were not successful, I believe, at least not quickly. And then there were the issues of the UN safe havens into 1993. But that is my understanding of operations in the Drina valley in late 1992. I don't doubt that the Muslim forces were conducting operations in there at that time and I believe that there were some burning and destruction and probably killing of Serbs in that area, but irrespective, what I can tell you is that operational directive was sent out in November 1992, as I've indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now that you've brought up that directive - but I hope that on Tuesday we'll shed more light on all of this - does that directive say that the army should leave, taking the people along, or the other way around? I understand that you may not be able to make a distinction because you don't know the Serbian language, but should the army leave with the people or should the people leave with the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to have directive four put up on the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the break. Feel free to do it during the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's take a break now. We'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just put one question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Objective one, do you distinguish between ethnic separation and state separation, ethnic on the one hand, state on the other?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible you could read directive one as a separation of states, but it would seem to me that other comments in the -- by yourself included, such as: We do not want to have large numbers of individuals in our state who are against that state; and comments by other delegates at the session who were talking about the issue of resettlement and the moving of Serbs and non-Serbs within Bosnia and also the seeming awareness or warning by General Mladic about this issue of resettlement, that this is not simply about the division of Bosnia into states, that there is going to be internal resettlement within RS territory. And it would seem to me that that was borne-out by a number of the Krajina Corps documents literally weeks later that we just discussed, individuals being moved into camps in large numbers, permanent deregistration references. It is possible if you take your comment with strategic goal number one on its own --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, we'll get to that, please, before the break do focus on whether I said separation of states there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] States --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- do not interrupt the witness from answering the question. You --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was not that comprehensive. My question was only whether there is a distinction between ethnic separation and state separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I agree with the witness expanding to some extent. Would you like -- do you wish to complete your answer, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

Mr. Robinson, we -- I think we have lost substantive -- substantial amount of time due to some amateurish style of questioning by the accused. If you could give him some advice as to how to put questions in relation to these kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we've discussed this, and I was actually thinking about if this issue of the erratas is going to go much further, it might be better to give the witness some homework and have the questioning on that topic resume on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be grateful for that. I can say immediately what the pages and paragraphs in my view were not amended. It is this one, so 1.113, 1.114 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let us wait and then let's deal with this questioning. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- have you read the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- pages --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or at least enough of it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take into account Judge Agius' position and did you enter appropriate corrections in the errata sheets as regards the second part of paragraph 1.113?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I did. I don't believe I did. And it was a long time ago when I did this and it wasn't something I remembered. I would be more than happy to take another look at it. I would be more than happy to look at the documents and the footnotes and I would be more than happy to amend the report if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you, then, to read out the numbers of paragraphs, 1.114. In the Brdjanin case you were asked about that at page 495, 496, and 497. That is Mr. Agius discussing there. It also includes pages 498 and 499 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness does not have access to e-court. Could you identify the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe if we could ask the witness to stay about five minutes after today and we can provide this information to him without taking up the Chamber's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's just what I was going to suggest, is that the Defence could print the pages of the transcript. I'd like a copy, too, since we're now in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that they could be given to the witness at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not have any objection to that step of action?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed in that way, then. Then let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This will be of much assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime we will add those - how many pages? - eight -- seven or eight pages to Exhibit D1932.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it will be more clear after -- I think it will be clearer on Tuesday after we have submitted our notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about a more important topic which goes to the gist of your report. It begins with paragraph 1.43. In that paragraph you say that - and you quote me - that it is [as interpreted] clearly indicated that non-Serb population was an enemy in the past and that they will continue to be an enemy . You can have a look at the entire paragraph. I hope you have it. Next you quote me. [In English] "Karadzic, himself, declared that 'We do not want to get a state which has a huge number of those who are against that state' ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, is this the basis on which you concluded that we were against the non-Serb part of the population?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the sole basis. I'm not sure I would phrase it that we were against the non-Serb population in that way. What I was saying is that you, yourself, at the 16th Assembly Session on more than one occasion indicated that the non-Serb population -- well, you stated that they were your historic enemy and would continue to be if they stayed in the same state, but you also indicated there was a danger of including in that state too many enemies who would work against that state. You also said in relation to territory that you didn't -- that we must also put an end to the Serbian megalomania of trying to include as many of our enemies in our areas as possible, especially as much territory as possible. And you also mention that we shouldn't take what is ours - that's a phrase that you used. So I didn't base it solely on the comments that you made but also on the comments that others made at that Assembly session. But then there clearly were the activities and comments in the Krajina Corps after this that led me to the impression that that was the case, that -- if you look at the language in the Krajina Corps instruction of the 21st, a morale report, it's very forceful language, it's very Serb-centric. I think I said that there wasn't too much tolerance in it. And I think when you put all those together as well as the notifications of what happened within weeks of this Assembly session, I think it was clear that the non-Serb population were seen as enemies and that there weren't to be many of them within Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Transcript page 91, lines -- I lost it. -- line 19 in the inverted comma it should read "Karadzic clearly indicated" instead of "it is clearly indicated." That sentence, if I draw your attention to that sentence in the 1.43, "Karadzic clearly indicated that non-Serb population had been their enemies in the past, were currently their enemies and would continue to be so if they remained within the same state," but I don't see any reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was when, Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic spoke about the strategic goals and when he articulated each of the goals in turn, he mentioned strategic goal 1, the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the Council for National Security which we have set up have formulated the strategic priorities, that is to say, the strategic goals for the Serbian people. "The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities - separation of states. Separation from those who are our enemies and who have continued --" sorry, "who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if they were -- if we were to stay together in the same state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let us try to shed some light on this. Did you realise that I was constantly advocating that Serbs should not take up more territory than rightfully belongs to them and that King Aleksandar was mistaken in wanting a great state, whereas other peoples did not want it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware that you constantly advocated that Serbs shouldn't take up more territory than rightfully yours, as in "constantly" being the operative phrase. Reading the 16th Session, I do think you do make comments about not taking territory that is not rightfully yours, presumably meaning rightfully Serb. I think one of the phrases you say after you've announced the strategic goals is this one: "We must also put an end to the Serbian megalomania of trying to include as many of our enemies in our areas as possible, especially as much territory as possible, as many hills and brooks, regardless of whether they are fertile or not." A number of the delegates at the Assembly session were talking about areas which may have been deemed difficult to take or hold or -- and maybe you were more cautious in that respect. As to the words "constantly advocating taking up of more territory than rightfully" yours, I can't comment on that. I do see that comment at the Assembly session and there was that comment about -- that we talked about earlier on in the military documents where soldiers were a bit unhappy about the possibility of having to trade back certain territory. But as to the phrase "constantly advocating taking territory that's not rightfully" yours, I can't really comment. I can say that there were some echos of that at the 16th Assembly Session, but the point of the Assembly session to me seemed to be it was a demarcation of what territory the leadership, including yourself, Mr. Karadzic, believed should be yours, meaning Serb. There was a phrase that you used as well not long after that quote about compact territory and, you know, need to have a compact -- a compact territory. Whether that helps or not, I don't know, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now: Do you know that before this session on the 18th of March, I accepted the idea that the Serbian constituent unit would have around 43 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that question can be answered with a yes or no. Do you know that I did accept that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that and I don't know the details. I know there were discussions with Mr. Cutileiro and plans being formulated in March and prior to that, in fact, but I'm not aware of that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you were able to ascertain that every deputy to the Assembly wanted his own constituency to be part of the Serbian Republic and that we had to include also all of the areas where the Serbs were a majority and I was fighting that sort of megalomania?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree one or two of the deputies at the 16th Assembly Session felt that they should have territory included. I think there's a reference to Tuzla at one stage, some of the areas up in the corridor, too, which were not predominantly Serb. But I wouldn't agree with you that you only included areas where Serbs were a majority. In fact, Prijedor, I believe, was not a municipality where Serbs were a majority. Bosanska Krupa was not a municipality where Serbs were a majority, as I remember. I think Sanski Most, it may have been even but maybe was not overwhelming Serb. I would have to check. And certainly as things developed in 1992, in the summer in particular, many of the municipalities that were not majority Serb were taken over irrespective. Some of the corridor municipalities were predominantly non-Serb. Doboj, I believe, was a municipality that was not predominantly Serb. So I would disagree with your view that you were only advocating - you, yourself, that is - from what I've read, you were only advocating that municipalities that were predominantly Serb were to be part of the RS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, would you agree that in the eventuality of a peaceful solution, the objectives would be one set, whereas in case of a solution by war there would be a different set of objectives? Just yes or no, is that understandable?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question in a yes-or-no manner, Mr. Karadzic. This -- if you're implying that the strategic goals were somehow simply political statements to be used in a political arena separate to what was going to be happening militarily, I would disagree with you completely. I think the strategic goals are echoed in the military documents. I think they formed the -- the footprint that was -- of the RS territory that the leadership wanted to control. There were reasons why they didn't control all of that at certain times through the whole conflict, but that was the aspiration. Those were not, to me, goals that were somehow meant for international negotiations alone. They may well have been part of international discussions that you or others may have had. I don't know. It's not part of my expertise. When I look at the goals, I see them as being a demarcation of the territory that the Bosnian Serbs wished to control. I see them forming very much a spine of many of the directives and certainly the directive one, to some degree three and four, in 1992, that I've reviewed. I can see echos from a military perspective of what they're expected to do in these goals. And in the Krajina in many -- in fact, probably all the areas from the Krajina Corps, they achieved their goal, they achieved the goal of a corridor and they took control of territory and held on to that territory almost until the end of the war when things -- things changed a bit in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's probably my fault that I'm not asking questions that are precise enough. I'll try better now. Do you know that before the war, in case of a peaceful solution we also had our proposal for the borders of those three constituent units. Do you know that the first Cutileiro map gave us a boundary on the Una River, on the Sava River, part of the Drina River, and part of the Neretva River? Is that right? If you didn't know, just say so, no problem.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of the Cutileiro agreement. That may well have been the case in part, but I also know that it wouldn't have given you the corridor link, for example. I don't believe the Cutileiro map gave the Serbs the cantonment and control in and around the corridor areas. I don't believe - I'm not sure about Sarajevo - but one of the strategic objectives in relation to Sarajevo was to divide Sarajevo into two, into a Serb part and a Muslim part. And I'm not sure Cutileiro was in agreement to that. But it isn't an area that I know of on expertise and I would defer to others about the detail of the Cutileiro maps and also the processes by which any agreements or not or made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The point is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. No objection. I just wanted to let my friends know I would like just a couple of minutes at the end to briefly address the Chamber on the motion -- the supplemental submission we received today to try to give you an update.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, then, that before the war, in case that war could be avoided and a political arrangement could be made, we had accepted that Sarajevo become a district and that we would not have the north corridor in Posavina. Do you understand that this is a plan that did not include either a compact territory or a link between the eastern and the western part of the Serb territory? You just indicated that. In case of a peaceful solution, the corridor would not be needed; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the various cantonments that were anticipated in the Cutileiro Plan did not include the corridor area predominantly as being under the Serb control. That -- that may have been the case. What I do know was that after Cutileiro was no longer an option, that the strategic goals - that we talked about that were referenced in preparation in early May in Mladic's diary on meetings on the 6th and 7th and also that were articulated on the 17th - were the goals that appeared to be taken by the military and used in relation to seizing control of territory deemed as Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the Vance-Owen Plan, which I had also accepted, we did not have a north corridor? Province number three had a considerable Croat majority. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the first Cutileiro map, the Muslim parts of municipalities Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc were envisaged as a separate canton, under their own administration?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of the maps. I do believe that Prijedor at least was -- was under Muslim authority, but I can't tell you the details for the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Brown, that the Serbian side in Bosanska Krupa controlled only the Serb areas on the right bank of the Una, whereas in Prijedor 80 per cent of the territory was under a Serb majority and the Serbs had proposed to Krupa, Una, and Prijedor, and Sanski Most to be divided into two municipalities each. Sarajevo already had 12 municipalities. Why not turn them into two municipalities, where each would have their own? And that proposal was still in force. It was on the table even when the war had already begun.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to Bosanska Krupa, all I can say is I know that come the 16th Assembly Session, the delegate there had made mention that the Muslims were no longer on -- in the municipality and had gone over the river into Croatia. Presumably the border of the Una was -- was seen as the border of the RS territory. There may well have been non-Serbs on the other side of the Una, but at least from Mr. Vjestica's comments, there weren't any Muslims by the 12th of May and operations that had occurred in there had included operations using the TO and the JNA. In relation to Prijedor, all I can say is I know that Prijedor municipality -- control was taken over in the 30th of April. We talked about Colonel Arsic, elements of -- or he provided assistance in that take-over in April. And we've already talked about the fact that the issue of weapons dead-lines led to attacks in late May and that many Muslims or non-Serbs in Prijedor were put into detention camps using -- in their own documentation by the end of May and beginning of June. And many of those eventually ended up in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to be more focused. You are saying that Vjestica had said that Muslims had disappeared from Bosanska Krupa municipality, that they had crossed the river into Croatia, whereas I'm putting it to you that the Krupa municipality stretches on both banks of the Una River. Most of the right side were Serbs. Most of the population on the left bank were Muslims. A large number of Muslims crossed over to the right bank in the same municipality, whereas Serbs evacuated their Muslims to Sanski Most within the same republic. Is that true? Do you consider it an expulsion when you move the population from one part of your municipality to another or from one part of your republic to another part?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only say what Mr. Vjestica said, which was that the Muslims had been moved to the other side of the Una River and there was no Muslims in his area and that he welcomed that, and he welcomed the fact that the Una River was now going to be a border. And I think his phrase was -- in fact, Mr. Vjestica says: "What are our adversaries doing? At the moment, they are all in the Cazin Krajina. On the right bank of the Una ... there are no more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa, all the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki Vrbovik," and a number of others, "we have evacuated them, so that there will be none there for the duration of the war. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely after our President told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border." So I draw the conclusion that Mr. Vjestica knows that the Muslims -- yes, maybe the municipality was split and maybe the river split the municipality, but certainly on the right bank that the Serbs wished to control, he indicates that there are no Muslims left and they had been evacuated over the river. And he seems to be quite pleased that with your announcement that the Una is going to be a strategic goal and will be the border of a new state, that these people were not going to be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can just say for our record, the section read out by Mr. Brown is from P956 pages 24 to 25 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, if he says Serb municipality Bosanska Krupa, what does that tell you? Doesn't that tell you that there is also a Muslim municipality? It was envisaged to have two municipalities. Why is he calling Bosanska Krupa a Serb municipality? Did you know that on the other side of the river there is also a municipality of Krupa?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may well be, Mr. Karadzic. But I think Mr. Vjestica is not talking about what's happening necessarily on the other side of the river. Mr. Vjestica is saying that there are no Muslims in the area that is to be a Serb territory and that the border of that Serb territory is to be on the Una River and, obviously, that he seems appreciative of the fact that he doesn't think they're going to be coming back now that there has been a declaration that that is the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, you cited yourself that there were none while the fighting is going on. Do you know that some Muslim villages were evacuated from Bosanska Krupa to Sanski Most, to another Serb territory, for the duration of the fighting? If you can answer this with a yes or no. Do you know that was the case?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it seems that Krupa was one of the early municipalities. There wasn't large-scale conflict going on in the Krajina when Mr. Vjestica was talking. There had been some take-overs of municipalities, including Prijedor. It wasn't the same in Krupa, it seems to me, as occurred later in May and into some other municipalities in June and July. Municipality of Krupa was taken over quite early, I believe, and he is indicating that -- that many Muslims of -- have been evacuated and that they aren't going to return. Nowhere do I see you, Mr. Karadzic, standing up and saying: Mr. Vjestica, this is unacceptable and this is not what we're doing in this Serb state. I don't see that at all. When he announces that so many people have been evacuated and believes they're not going to -- the happy news that this is our border and they will not return, I don't see you, Mr. Karadzic, standing up and saying: I think you've got the wrong end of the stick here. This is not what we're meant to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will show you on Tuesday what exactly I said there and in many other places at many other times. Do you continue to claim that the Serbs occupied Bosanska Krupa or they took control only of their own territories in Bosanska Krupa? It is a small distinction when they took only their own Serb municipality on the right bank of the river where they were a majority, whereas the Muslim part of Bosanska Krupa was on the other side of the Una River and nobody touched it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may be true that they took control -- if I can finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellent --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it may be true that they took control of the part that they believed was theirs which was up onto the Una River and it may well have been that there were Muslim enclaves on the other side that they didn't believe were to be part of RS territory. But what it seems to be is that the enclaves of Muslims inside the territory of Krupa that was controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities, those Muslims were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Brown? Where were they evacuated, within the same municipality or within the same republic, to Sanski Most, for instance?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Vjestica says they had been evacuated over the river. Irrespective of where they've gone, they appear no longer to be living in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at ET 93-111. Yesterday there was talk about Mladic's diary, where I speak of the mistakes made by King Aleksandar. Just to show you how translation works, in the English translation it said that I said if we are going to take care of our own territories and our own people, whereas I claim I said: Do we care for territories or do we care for people, again in my efforts to dissuade those who wanted large territories. That's P01 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you are not giving your evidence. Let's upload the document and put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a split screen with English on the one side and the manuscript on the other side. That's ET 93-111. The English translation -- that's the English translation, 93-111, and the number of the document is 01478. The Serb is 94 or perhaps 96. P01478. Or maybe it's P01477. But I think it was said yesterday that it was 478. Now we need 96, three pages down in the manuscript. And in English it's from 93 to 111. English 93, Serbian 94 in the manuscript -- no, it's 97 in English, two pages further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 97 for English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in Serbian I need three pages further in the manuscript. [In English] 3272 [Interpretation] That's the ERN number, the last digits of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this passage, Mr. Brown, where I advocate that territories should not become a fetish and I say King Aleksandar got a large state but lost Serbia. That was paid for by lives. What do we care for more, territories or the people? Can you see that I am in favour of the people against territories?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't necessarily agree that that section says that at all. I agree that you say -- you pose the question: "What is it that we care about: Territory or people?" But it seems to me one -- that when you put them all together, that your position is one that you articulate at the Assembly session, is that: It's territory that we need to control. And if we are in the business of wherever the Serbs are, we have to control that area, we might come -- we might -- if the territory's too large, we might lose. King Aleksandar got a large state and lost Serbia. "We paid for this with our lives. "What is it that we care about: Territory or the people?" Posing the question. "If we Serbs," I think that is probably "do not start." "If we Serbs do not start thinking about a state and about our territory, then we will lose." And then there is other discussions about: "According to the map we have 66 per cent of the territory which the world would deny us." So it seems to me that the discussion here is one of: If we're not careful and do what we've done in the past, which is to get such a large territory, maybe in places where Serbs are a minority or that maybe are not deemed as historically Serb, then we might have the same problem as happened in the past, which is that we will lose the state all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that I wasn't discussing the people living in Republika Srpska because King Aleksandar and his state included Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the peoples of those countries were not in favour of a unified state and it cost us in 1941. Don't you see that this was not discussing ethnic divisions? I was in favour of being modest in terms of territory and I was criticised for having suggested that we give up 20 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of this is that there is a discussion at the senior level about what should be the defined borders of the RS state, and it may well have been that others felt that borders should be more expansive. Maybe others felt that wherever Serbs were, that that should be part of the state. And it may well be that you are saying: Historically, if we make our state so big, we may not be able to hold on to it and that we need to be realistic. I don't think it's talking about looking after people particularly. I think it's about defining in this discussion what the parameters and the borders of the state are. And maybe others have a more expansive view and you have a different view. And I think you're bringing to the attention of this meeting that: If we're not careful and we take too big a territory, we might go the same way as you highlight King Aleksandar, who loses the state all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was not a stenograph, but Mladic's notes and that he merely made short notes of what the people said? He didn't write down everything. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a notebook, Mr. Karadzic, and it would seem to be that there are bullet points here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for today. We'll resume ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I totally forgot. I'm sorry, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be quick and I don't think it matters, this has nothing to do with the witness's testimony. We received a supplemental submission today. I don't know if this issue has already been decided by the Chamber. If not, it would be moot and I will sit down and be quiet. I just wanted to let you know that what we are doing now -- we will try to respond very quickly to this supplemental submission. The real issue here would be confidential exhibits, and what we're trying to do is match up however many confidential exhibits were included in that -- in the Tolimir case, point 2 of what the submission requests in paragraph 4. And we believe, just from the initial review -- and I think that we will find that virtually all of the confidential exhibits in that case will likely have been disclosed previously as part of our disclosure in this case. So it, in fact, may not be any problem at all. I won't identify which are which, but it may, in fact, be that there is nothing or very little that the Defence does not have access to and has not had access to for a year, and we will come back to Your Honours and to our -- to the Defence as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think we can hear from you on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we're trying to -- it's not all up to Mr. Reid, but I think we're going to try to get an accurate answer today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if the Prosecution could also advise us how many confidential Defence exhibits there are and if we have received any of those because that's also a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It will be both, Your Honour. We'll do our audit for both categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume on Tuesday at 2.15. Have a nice weekend, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of November, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.
